utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, before we get on with the evidence, there are one or two procedural matters that I must ask the Chamber to deal with pretty well immediately. It may be that if I identify the issues now, either as to all or some, the Chamber would think it most helpful to come back to them later in the morning, either at the beginning of the last session or at the end of last session, although dealing with things at the end of the last session is always a problem because we always run out of time. The first three matters are very short and can be dealt with in public session and then there are two very short -- two matters to be dealt with, with your leave, in private session. The first, then, topic is the 92 bis applications or the 92 bis position as to certain witnesses. I sought to raise the issue of Mr. Hendrie yesterday and got it wrong. The position is that his first but not his second statement have been approved for 92 bis, and though Mr. Ryneveld will be taking and can deal with that, we would be grateful for your ruling in relation to that. Next Monday, K6 returns.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: On whom we've already made a ruling.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And -- yes. He's returning and, as I understand it, will be able to give evidence with facial distortion and pseudonym. The question arises as to the 92 bis potential for that witness. William Walker arrives on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just pausing there. I think from our usual rulings in respect of witnesses of that type, I would be inclined to say that he was someone who should give evidence live.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As Your Honour pleases. In effect, if the Chamber changes its mind or expresses a different view, perhaps you'd be good enough to let us know. William Walker has made himself available at short notice and at personal inconvenience to come on Sunday night, I think, for arrival after a long jet flight here, on Monday morning, with a view to being taken as a witness on Tuesday. We would be asking the Chamber to consider those parts of his statement that may cover territory already covered by others to be subject to 92 bis and to save valuable court time and to minimise the inconvenience to him. Perhaps we can return to those issues. But insofar as they are outstanding, that would be Walker, I suspect, at the end of the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, if we granted 92 bis for those parts that you think are, forgive the expression, 92 bis'able, how long would his examination-in-chief be?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll have to come back to you on that later this morning as well. If you'll give me leave to come back on that; I can't give an actual estimate at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We ought clearly, then, to deal with Witness K6 on Monday, if at all possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: K6 on Monday. There are implications for others who have to look after him and so on. And that, incidentally, may involve -- yes, I'm grateful for being reminded. It's possible that that would involve putting back two witnesses, Ramadani and Avdyli, although I'm anxious not to do so because they've already been here in The Hague for some time. Depends on whether we get through to them today. Unlikely. Can we go into private session for two topics?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Will it be sensible to deal with Mr. Hendrie's second statement, and also -- on the 92 bis point? And also, I have in mind the statements of Messrs. Jemini, Popaj, Ramadani, and Avdyli as being admissible under Rule 92 bis and it might be sensible to take them all. Yes. Well, subject to anything the accused has to say on the matter - and he should be heard - we propose to admit the statements of Mr. Hendrie, both statements, and the statements of those witnesses I've read out, under Rule 92 bis. Mr. Milosevic, is there anything you want to say about that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a general remark to make in view of the fact that my cross-examination time has been shortened by your 92 bis Rule where statements are given in writing, testimony is given in writing, that this very seriously limits my possibilities of cross-examining the witnesses in the interests of truth. And the second point is that I still haven't received William Walker's statement. I hear that he's going to be here on Tuesday, is he? It's Friday today, as you well know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will raise that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thirdly, my third point: You still haven't given me an answer, although I asked you twice, you promised to respond, to my question, the following: My associate who has taken it upon himself to calculate all this, told me that we received 70.000 pages of documents this week, 200 videotapes, some 50-odd audiotapes, and I don't know what else, not counting all the little bits and pieces that I find on my table here this morning. But my question was to you: When do you expect me to read through those 70.000 pages, look at the 200 videotapes and listen to the 50 audiotapes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And the answer is this, as I told you: It's a matter which we are considering. The window of opportunity, if I can use that expression, will occur in the summer. We shall stop sitting on the Kosovo case on the 26th of July. There will be then at least three weeks, and we'll consider the necessary time for you to prepare for the other matter. Now, it may be that Croatia and Bosnia can be split. I'm not sure if it can in terms of preparation or whether in fact they are so entwined that it can't be.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm happy to give some preliminary indications but loath to take time. I think the Chamber and the accused may be helped by knowing that my intention is to have a list of witnesses prepared for both cases. I hope to have a reasonably accurate running list of witnesses to be prepared by about the end of next week, and I suspect that you will find that a very large number of those witnesses in the early stages will cover both cases. Therefore, splitting them in any hermetic way might not be realistic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And you will indicate, will you, what -- which of those witnesses could be subject to Rule 92 bis?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly. Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We are moving some way now from the point. So the answer is, Mr. Milosevic, that we have in mind that question of time and your having the necessary time to prepare for the next stage of the case. We will admit the statements under Rule 92 bis. Returning to Mr. Walker, when will the statement be available?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll find out the detail of service, if there's been no service, and come back to it later this morning, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, clearly something should be available tonight or earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So the accused can have it over the weekend. It may be convenient, before we go into closed or private session, to deal with the documents we've been handed, the exhibits, the outstanding exhibits which the accused asked to be admitted. They are numbered D14, 18, is there a 19? D14 to D19. Now, unless there's any Prosecution objection, we propose to admit them. We will go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, our records reveal that Ambassador Walker's statement of the 16th of May of 1999 was part of the supporting material disclosed in respect of the indictment. The second statement, unsigned, our records show to have been disclosed on the 27th of May. I'll check for receipts in respect of that over the breaks. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Have you got some copies?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We can sort that out by the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Are we in open session?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, we are.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: The Prosecution calls Ian Robert Hendrie.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Mr. Hendrie, could you tell the Court your full name, please.

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: Ian Robert Hendrie.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And, Mr. Hendrie, do I understand correctly, sir, that you are currently 42 years old?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And you have a background as a detective in both the Royal Hong Kong and the London Metropolitan Police forces; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: It is, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, sir, did there come a time in 1997 or 1998 when you served one of the offices of the United Nations in the Balkans?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: Between October 1997 to October 1998, I served in the International Police Task Force in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And later on, in December of 1998, were you involved with the OSCE/KVM mission?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: In November 1998, I joined the United Kingdom Diplomatic Observer Mission and then joined the OSCE in December of 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, sir, I'd ask you to direct or focus your remarks at this point to an incident on the 16th of January, 1999. Did something happen that day that took you to the village of Racak?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: I was informed on the morning of the 16th that an incident had taken place at a village of Racak on the previous day.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And did you, in fact, as a result of that information, travel to Racak along with other individuals?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: I did, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And just very briefly, I'd ask you to tell us what you did when you got there.

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: We arrived at about midday at a checkpoint of the KLA on the edge of the village. After negotiating through the checkpoints, I was shown around the village and saw various sites where I saw bodies. I photographed and made observations on what I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Your Honours, in view of the 92 bis procedure, I propose now to read a brief summary contained in paragraphs 3 through 13, and then I want to return for a few questions under paragraph 14.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: You took a number of photographs, as you've indicated.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Your Honours, you will find that those photographs are contained in the Racak binder, binder 1 of 5, which have been marked an exhibit, and they can be found immediately behind tab 5 of that binder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Have we got an exhibit number for the statements?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I have a couple of questions on that yet, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, sir, you gave statements to the members of the ICTY firstly on the 25th of February 1999; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And you attended before a presiding officer of the Tribunal on the 11th of February, 2002 and indicated or made a solemn declaration that that statement was true and correct to the best your information, knowledge, and belief?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Did you also give a second statement, on the 15th of December, 2000, and go through the same solemn declaration proceedings on the 28th of May of this year?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: Yes, I did, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Might those exhibits -- or those statements be given exhibit numbers at this point.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 214 and 214 [sic] for the redacted version. Excuse me, 214A for the redacted version.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, by way of a very brief summary: In his statements, the witness indicates that he was originally -- initially shown the body of someone identified to him as Banush which reports in his statement at scene 1. Now, for benefit of the Court and in terms of some diagrams and I believe the large maps that were in these court proceedings taken by Mr. Kelly, those are referred to on those documents as CL1, that's location one, scene 1. I just thought I would relate the scenes in his statement to the other descriptors that you have. He was shown a uniformed KLA soldier -- by a KLA soldier, a courtyard where a man named Bidi Banush identified the headless body of Azem Banush, and later, at the morgue, this body was labelled as RA-1. Then he was at scene 2, which is location 2, scenes 2 and 3. A man maimed Ismail Beqiri informed him of the location of the bodies of three brothers, Arif, Sabri, and Haki Syla, who had all been shot. A short distance from this location, he was shown the body of Hajriz Jakujsi, who had also been shot. At scene 3, which is location 2, scene 4, he was brought to a family compound consisting of two houses where the body of Ahmet Mustafa, who was apparently around 70 years old, was identified to him. He appeared to have been shot several times and was later identified with the morgue label RA-9. At scene 4 in his statement, which is location 2, scene 5 in the other documents, he was shown the body of a male in his mid-30s, identified to him as Skender, who had part of his skull missing. He examined an axe that was nearby which appeared to have a small amount of blood on it. At the entrance gate to that compound, he found a skull fragment with some hair on it; and in the house, he found bone fragments that appeared consistent with the man's injuries. This house had suffered heavy gunfire damage. En route to the next location, he located and photographed a rifle grenade in the ground with a fintail protruding. At scene 5 in his statement, which is location 5, scene 10 in other documentation, he came across a freshly-dug trench which was about four feet deep and two feet wide which showed no evidence of recent use. He then came to a gully where he located a total of 22 bodies in two groups, one comprising 15 bodies and the second comprising seven bodies. There was a 23rd body located a short distance away but in the same vicinity. On the northern side of the gully, he found ammunition boxes labelled in Cyrillic, indicating 7.6 calibre ammunition. Now, this witness, in his statement, indicates that there were no signs of drag marks or blood leading in or out of the gully. It was apparent, however, to him that some if not all of the bodies had been turned over. Bloodstaining indicated the location where death occurred. All the bodies were rigid and dressed in civilian clothing. There were no weapons near the bodies. The vast majority of injuries on all the bodies he saw in Racak that day were due, in his opinion, to gunshots. He then recorded the individual details of bodies at scene 5, 1 to 23, which you will find again referred to as location 5, scene 10. He moves on then to crime location 3, scene 7. From the gully, he walked into the village to a house with the number 30 on it where the body of Hanemshah Mehmeti was identified to him. Mehmeti was reportedly killed by a sniper while Mehmeti was going to the aid of someone already hit by a sniper. He was then taken to another location and shown the area where Bajram and Hanemshah Mehmeti were killed. The body of Bajram was identified to him. It was lying in a room of the family home. He did not photograph that body because he'd used up all his film, however, another OSCE member by the name of Michael Pedersen apparently videoed it. He then moves on to what was referred to in Mr. Kelly's documentation as location 4, scene 9, which is a family compound where the bodies of Riza, Halim, and Zenel Beqiri were lying in a room. Villagers told this witness that they were shot by the police from a hill about 60 metres away. He also did not photograph those bodies. Xhemzjl Beqiri, a survivor from that incident, told the witness what happened. He moved on then to location 3, scene 8. He was brought to another location where he was shown a compound that had a ten-foot wall surrounding four houses. Ismet Bahimi pointed out the body and severed head of his brother Ajad Bahimi. Apparently he had been shot first and then, sometime later, his head was removed. He did not photograph this scene. There was damage to the family tractors and it appeared that the house had been ransacked. In his statement, he also talks about his dealings on the 17th of January, 1999, with Judge Marinkovic. He was at Stimlje when he saw a build-up of Serbian forces that were there apparently to assist the investigating Judge, Ms. Marinkovic. Her purpose was to enter Racak to investigate the incident. The witness indicates that there were sporadic firing aimed at and around the village. On the 18th of January, 1999, the witness spoke with Judge Marinkovic in relation to the investigation into Racak. She stated, inter alia, that the purpose of her visit was to show the world that the bodies were not of innocent peasants, as Walker had said, but that they were terrorists. She - and this is my paraphrasing - said that they found evidence that proves the villagers were terrorists because they found uniforms, trenches, machine-guns, and bombs. He then, in his statement, goes on to indicate attending at the mortuary on the 19th and 20th of January, 1999, to observe the post-mortems of some of the deceased persons from Racak performed by the forensic pathologist from both Pristina and from Belorussia. He videoed some of those proceedings. Now, Your Honours, I propose at this point to show five photographs to assist the Trial Chamber with respect to evidence heard from witnesses concerning their observation of bodies and their conclusions that the bodies had been mutilated, shot at close range, or decapitated. You will recall that there's been extensive cross-examination about that, and in fairness and to assist the Trial Chamber to see whether or not there was any basis for those comments by the witnesses, I propose to show first of all photograph 00732320. And Mr. Usher, if you could put that on the ELMO. This is a photograph showing an unusual eye injury. You will recall evidence about witnesses talking about mutilation and eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Witness, I'd like you to look at that photograph. Do you recognise the scene depicted in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes. Now, is this one of the photographs you took or is this just a photograph of a scene that you recall when you were there on the 16th of January?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: It's one of the photographs I took.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. And -- all right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: The next photograph, please. Yes. Photograph 00732364. These are all in the Racak binder, in sequence, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Again, Mr. Hendrie, is this one of the photographs you took?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: It is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Below and behind the right ear, there appears to be a mark. Can you describe what that mark looks like?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: It appears to be an entry gunshot wound with scorching and stippling around the wound.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: In your statement, sir, you indicated that they appeared to have been shot at close range; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Is this one of the factors that you considered in coming to that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: It is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you. Next photograph, 00732368. Again, sir, that's a photograph you took?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And what, if anything, can you tell us about this photograph in relation to the eye area?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: It appears that a bullet has entered the skull and the passage of the bullet has caused the eyes to be distorted.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you. Next photograph, 00732387. Again, sir, is this a photograph that you took?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: We've heard evidence, sir, about mutilation of bodies and gaping holes in the chest area. What, if anything, did you note about this particular body when you photographed it?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: I observed that there were two or what appears to be two gunshot wounds to the chest and fluids and remains of internal organs on the chest.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And this area that you noted that's shown in this photograph, where is that wound in relation to where you would normally expect to find the heart?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: It was in the same vicinity.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And finally, Your Honours, a photograph which has not yet been marked as an exhibit in these proceedings. Oh, you've got it there? Yes. Would you put that on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: That appears to be a headless torso, sir. You, in your report, indicated you saw two of them. Did you take this photograph?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: I can't recall just now.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. Do you recall whether or not you saw any headless bodies while you were being shown around Racak on the 16th of January, 1999?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: There were two, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Did you photograph one or two or any?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: One.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Finally, Your Honours, I'd like to show a 30-second clip of Exhibit 95. You've already seen certain portions of it. Could the AV booth help us? Start the video. It's only about 30 seconds. This is at a part of the exhibit, Your Honours, 95, of the video that was taken with Mr. Walker present. Yes. Would you run the video, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: "Okay. At the top of the hill. The first corpse is that of a male, probably in his mid-to-late-30s. He appears to have been executed by being shot at close range through the head. There are two indicators of -- "One of the bullets -- "There are two indicators of exit wounds. The man appears to have had his right ear severed. He has been shot at very close range in both the face, and I can't see where the chest exit wound originated. "There's a bullet. I just wanted to assess what kind it is. "Okay. "Because it's not fired. It's pretty big. "Got me? "Yeah. "There are significant numbers of 7.62 cardboard boxes sprinkled around the area, suggesting that those that undertook this calmly executed their victims and reloaded in the same place."

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Stop the video there, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, the photograph of the body that we see -- I'm sorry, the image of the body that we see in the video, is that the same person that you photographed?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: It is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. And again, it showed the chest wound?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: It did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Ryneveld, you --

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you. We haven't marked yet -- we haven't given a number to that last photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, but I -- I want to know who that was.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Sorry. That was a -- I can ask the witness, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Witness, did you recognise that individual who was speaking on camera as having been present on the 16th of January when you were there?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I didn't see the man there on the day in question. However, I did recognise him as being a man named Brown, a British liaison officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And were you aware of his function as head of the medical team there or were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, it would be better if you called Mr. Brown.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes. That's fine. Thank you, Your Honour. Those are all the questions, other than having that last photograph, which has not been entered, marked as an exhibit, those are my questions. Might that be given an exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 215.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Hendrie, a technical question: The images that we saw were of apparently internal organs, some of them, spread out over the bodies or elsewhere near to the bodies. All of that would have resulted from shooting at close range or could have resulted from being shot at such close range?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It could have, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Because I must say that, looking at it, one would have the impression that the organs were pulled, were taken out almost manually, which is consistent with what some of the witnesses said. But what you're saying is that that is also consistent with being shot at very close range?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, first of all, I have an objection since here we heard comments on details which are considered to be an exclusive domain of forensic analysis, and this witness here is not a forensic expert. I think that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Why don't you ask him about his qualifications?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I can see that he's a police detective. He worked in the English police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Hendrie. Help us about your qualifications to deal with this evidence. What is your background in forensic matters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I served as a detective in the Royal Hong Kong Police for six years, dealing with murders and rapes and other serious crimes, and I've served in the Metropolitan Police Service in London for some 13 years and the last few years as a detective. And I served in Bosnia and in Kosovo where I've dealt with and seen numerous gunshot wounds and have worked with forensic pathologists and scientists on similar cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that is the whole point of my comments. You have statements of forensic experts, and here you are taking evidence on the same subject from a witness who is not an expert. But let me turn to my questions. First of all, I would like to clarify something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Before you do, it's right that we should deal with your comment. Any question of qualification or appropriateness of this witness to deal with the matters which he does are matters which go to the weight of his evidence, nothing else. You can cross-examine him about the matter. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, my time is extremely limited, and since you classified this witness as a 92 bis -- am I understanding this correctly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. You've got an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, in that case, concerning the previous topic, are you, sir, a medical expert at all?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. You know quite well he's not. He's given his background.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this is exactly what I claimed, and you told me to ask him about his qualifications, and this is why I put this question to him. But all right. Let's turn to other issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But before we focus on specific issues, let me ask you the following: In several instances in your statement, for example on page 1, you say that you saw people in black uniforms and then you say in camouflage uniforms. It was the KLA soldiers in the village. And then you go on to say: "I don't know how many other soldiers I saw that day," and then, at the bottom of the page, you say that you were told that the KLA had removed the bodies of the soldiers before the MUP forces and the VJ forces arrived, which, of course, is illogical. And at that point, you say that you cannot remember how you obtained this information, and you also cannot remember the identity of the persons who gave you this information. And then you go on to say that you don't know the identity of any of the KLA soldiers or military police and so on. So for example, on page 5, you say: "I'm not in the position to confirm the source of the information." This is the spot where you talk about the detaining of the civilian population. And then on page 6, you talk about mass graves near Orahovac where the remains of some missing persons --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, I just quoted seven or eight instances in your statement where you say that you do not have information about locations or the source of the information given to you. So that means that a number of allegations stated by you here is something that you don't know the source for. So is it something that is logical for a professional policeman to state? So you say on a number of occasions that you don't know the identity, you don't know the source of information, and so on. Is it logical for a policeman to state something of this kind?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Do you think you can deal with that or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I reported what I was told as faithfully as I could. It is correct that I do not know or cannot recall the identity of some of the sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, when you are retelling something that you were told and you cannot remember or you don't know the source of the information, isn't that something that in lay terms we describe as hearsay, rumours?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: I believe that's a matter for the Court, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's clarify another issue. You said that when you came to Racak, you were stopped by the members of the KLA who were dressed in special black uniforms, well-armed, and so on; is that right? This is what it says here. "They wore black uniforms with KLA insignia. They were well-armed," and so on. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is correct except I didn't say that they were special.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I quoted your words. "Black uniforms, and they were well-armed."

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't normally interject, but if the witness is purporting -- I'm sorry -- if the accused is purporting to quote to the witness a direct quote, then at least the English translation of that doesn't use the words "well-armed," it says "armed with" and then describes it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I think that should be put to the witness accurately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Quite right. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in that case, I would like you to look at the Serbian version, which says "well-armed." I did not read the English version, and I cannot look into a crystal ball to see whether the English and Serbian versions are identical. I think it's the responsibility of those who provide this material to me. But my question is as follows: I would like you to check the Serbian version and see that it says "well-armed." I did not invent this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What language did you make your statement in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: English, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, just looking at the statements of 24th of May, there is the word "well-armed" used under the 16th of January.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Second paragraph. Page 2 of the statement served 24th of May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Which statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's the interview of 12/10/2000 and 17/10/2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have found the location. First of all, in the first statement, it refers to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's the second statement. It seems to be the second statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes. And I acknowledge that although in the first statement, it simply says "armed with," that in the second statement in paragraph -- in the now paragraph numbered -- is it 2? I'm sorry, I'm having trouble finding it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's page 197181 on the top right-hand corner, second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes, I see it now. The number 2, it does say -- he's now referring back to his first statement and says: "They were well-armed but the weaponry did not appear to be different." So I see that, depending on which statement you're looking at, one statement simply says "armed" and the second statement says "well-armed." I accept that, and I apologise.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. I accept Mr. Ryneveld's apologies, by I think that, Mr. May, you cannot draw a conclusion immediately that what the other side says is correct and what I say is incorrect. I think that that is one more manifestation of complete bias that we have seen here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Move on, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The people in the black uniforms who were well-armed, were they the same kind of people that were seen on the different photographs and images accompanying Mr. Walker on various occasions during the Verification Mission's term of office?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can you answer that or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I cannot.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Who informed you about the occurrences in Racak? But let's be expeditious, brief. I'll ask short questions, you give me short answers to make the best use of our time.

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: The head of the Human Rights Division, Sandra Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Sandra Mitchell. All right. And you were told that there were a large number of fatalities, human fatalities. Now, do you remember what the figure that was quoted was? How many fatalities?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: At that time, Your Honour, it was just a large number.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Ken Marcusson from the local KVM unit told you that on the 15th of January he was at a certain position close to Racak. That is to say that he was in the same position which is where the tanks, as you said, of the Yugoslav army and the snipers were located; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that the Yugoslav authorities had previously informed the representatives of the KVM of the activities and called them to perform their functions as observers?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: I can't answer that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did Marcusson tell you how long the operation lasted and when the members of the police and army withdrew from Racak?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: Mr. Marcusson just referred to the incident of the previous day lasting the day. He did not tell me at what time the security forces withdrew.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And where did you arrive at Stimlje or Racak from on the 16th of January? Where were you coming from?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: Pristina, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In passing through Stimlje or Racak, did you notice members of the army or the police force, either nearby or at a further distance?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: I don't recall seeing any security forces on my journey, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So the only forces that you did see were the KLA forces that stopped you at their checkpoint; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can confirm that I did see members of the KLA. I cannot recall whether I did see any security forces on that day or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How many KLA members were at the checkpoint, manned the checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: About a dozen, Your Honour. Sorry, 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Twelve of them. Now, you claim that after a short argument, you were allowed to enter Racak. What argument was this about?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wouldn't term it an argument, it was a discussion or negotiation for us to enter. It referred to the ethnicity of the driver and interpreter that we had with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So on the 16th of January, the village of Racak and the surrounding parts were under the military control of the KLA, weren't they? Right?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: I believe so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you have any idea as to the number of KLA members in Racak and surrounding parts on that day? Do you have any idea?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I'm sorry. No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that on the 16th of January, your colleague, Michael Pedersen, filmed with a video camera the locations that you describe and the victims. When did he arrive in the village?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: I don't know, Your Honour. He arrived after I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How soon after you?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: I don't know, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did he come alone or did he come with anybody else?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: When I saw him, Your Honour, he was alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In your statement, you say that on the 16th of January, when you were touring some places in Racak and the surrounding parts that you mention in your statement, that KLA -- a KLA soldier led you in a camouflage uniform and elderly man, that these were the people who escorted you on your tour; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: A KLA soldier in camouflage uniform did show us in the initial stages, and we were shown different locations by different members of the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that when you investigated the scene of the event, as you denote to be place, spot number 1, Azem Banushi, did you notice a pistol casing of a 7.62 calibre type?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: There was an empty case of 7.62 calibre, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: A pistol one; right?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: I believe they're used in semi-automatic or automatic weapons as opposed to a pistol.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Look at page 3, paragraph 2 of your statement, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It may not follow because the accused is using the Serbian. What is the passage, Mr. Milosevic, that you want this witness to deal with?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: English page 3, end of second paragraph, first statement.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. I don't think that observation is one I'm challenging.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But in view of your experience and as you explained to us, you dealt with killings during your long career, can you make an assumption as to who could have shot the bullet which that casing -- which left that casing?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you claim that the photographs of this scene indicate the absence of any signs of armed battle. Is that what you're saying? Do you claim that the photographs that you showed indicate the absence of any signs of armed battle?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: My observation was that there was no indication of armed fighting at that location.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you exclude the possibility of an armed battle, the participation of these individuals in an armed battle; right? Or do you just say on that scene, in that location?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you don't follow the question, say so, Mr. Hendrie.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry. Would Mr. Milosevic repeat the question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Of course. You exclude, therefore, the possibility of any armed battle in which these individuals could have participated, or do you just exclude the possibility of armed battle in that particular locality?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: Your Honour, nothing I saw or observed on that day indicated that the people -- the dead bodies that I had seen had been engaged in combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what should you have seen in order to confirm that they had been engaged in armed combat? What should they have looked like, the dead people, having been killed in combat? What should they have looked like?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's not just what the combatants, if that's what they were, would look like, it's actually other indications in the vicinity. Empty cases, weapons, discarded munitions, damage from the use of those munitions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. So you go back to the location. Like you said a moment ago, you said location. Now, can that mean that those participants in armed combat were brought to that location where there was no armed battle or combat?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: Your Honour, nothing that I observed on that day indicated that the bodies of the men and child and woman had died at another location other than those ones where I was actually told and shown that the body had been moved and the location where the body had been taken from.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, if the bodies had been moved, the bodies which are moved -- the bodies could have been brought in from somewhere. Isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: I don't believe so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How do you know what distance these bodies were moved from, whether they were moved five metres or 50 metres or perhaps 200 metres? How could you tell?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: I spoke to various people and was shown and observed different locations which indicated where people had died and then where they had been moved to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did they explain to you how these people had in fact died?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: On some occasions, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And in that ditch or gully where you saw the bodies, did they show you that?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: I was shown a number of bodies in the gully, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did they tell you that at the top of the gully was the police, who allegedly fired at those people?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: They didn't tell you that story, did they?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How long did you stay in that location?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: Which location?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The place where you explained that, in your opinion, there were no traces of armed battle, as you explained it, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: Your Honour, are we referring to the first location, the first body?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Which location?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, let's say the first. How long were you in the first location?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: I couldn't say, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: How long were you at the scene in the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Until the late afternoon, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't think we have what time you got there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About midday, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In describing location 2 on page 3, you say that you examined the bodies of three males. Could you describe to us how you conducted this examination?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: Initially, I observed the bodies from a distance, approached, and then visually observed each body in turn and then attempted to turn the body over to examine, to see whether there were any injuries on their backs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you say that in addition to the -- next to the bodies of these three men, you saw no empty casings. Does that mean that no firearms were used?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. It just means that there were no empty casings near those two bodies -- I'm sorry, three bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, how much time went by, in your opinion, from the moment of death to the moment you actually saw the bodies?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: I can't say that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the soldier that took you on this tour, he knew where he was taking you, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: I believe so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that the KLA, before you examined all these places with the team, that you -- that they had access to the bodies?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And are you aware of a report of the aluminum test with the paraffin glove from the hands of people who were killed in Racak?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: I am aware that the paraffin test was applied to the deceased.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know of the results, what the results were?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And were you interested in learning the results at all?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: I would have been, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you never asked to hear them?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Serb authorities were cooperative -- sorry, less than cooperative with the OSCE in this matter. I do make an observation that I believe the paraffin test has been discredited a number of years ago in the United States and elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. And that was the evidence in this case from an expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You claim that next to the bodies - on page 4, you say that, paragraph 1 - that you saw a pool of blood, and it was the body belonging to Hajriz Jakujsi; right?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: There was a pool of blood next to the deceased Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And is it true that the blood hadn't dried?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Would you like to look at your statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, I don't know whether you can find it for us. Judge Kwon has it. It's page 4, second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The pool of blood by the body of Hajriz Jakujsi.

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: It was still moist, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that it was well suited to a chemical analysis?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: You could subject dried and fluid blood to analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you claim that the blood belonged to the victims that you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you take any blood samples to analyse them or to perform comparative analyses with the victims?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. The OSCE had no such facilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So on the basis of what do you say that the blood on the ground belonged to the victims?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: In this particular case, I cannot say categorically that the blood on the ground adjacent to the deceased was his blood.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you claim that the body of Hajriz Jakujsi was moved in respect to its initial position. That's right; isn't it?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: It appeared that the body had been rolled over, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know the original position of his body or, rather, do you know what position the body of this man was in when death occurred?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: The -- the body appeared to have been rolled over from a -- lying front down and rolled over on his back. The blood did correspond to the injuries of the deceased.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So your answer to my question as to whether you know the original position of the body was a positive response; right? It was yes.

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: I cannot say that I know. I can say that I believe from my observations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. If the -- if you don't know the original position of the body, does that allow -- does that allow, along with the fact that the body was moved, that death did not occur in the place where you saw the body for the first time?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: I don't believe so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You don't believe so.

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: No, sir. Sorry. No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you don't exclude the possibility or do you fully exclude it?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: Your Honour, there were no indications that the body had been moved from another location and placed where I had seen it. There were no drag marks. There were no blood trails. The pool of blood I saw corresponded to the injury if the body had been face down and then rolled over.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: If the body were brought in part of a tent, for example, tent canvas, would there be drag marks or blood traces when it was brought in?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: I believe there would be indications that the body had actually been brought in, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, as you are a policeman with 20 years of experience at your job, can you say that you're a specialist for certain aspects of your profession?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: I'm not sure I'd describe myself as a specialist, Your Honour, but certainly knowledgeable in certain areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you move the bodies you examined?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: Some of them, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that it is a basic rule of the profession to which you belong that on the scene, nothing should be touched or moved until an official investigation is conducted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is it a basic rule?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In normal circumstances, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And why were these abnormal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was not there as a police officer. I was there as a member of the OSCE to observe what had occurred and to draw some conclusions. There had been some conflict the previous day. The KLA were in possession of the village and the security forces were likely to want to re-enter the village, which is actually what did occur a couple of days later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When you talk about bodies from scene 2 and the Syla brothers - it is the fourth paragraph on page 3 - you make no mention of traces of blood on the ground; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was there any blood around their bodies or not?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: Not that I observed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And the absence of blood next to bodies with numerous gunshot wounds, does that mean or can that mean that these people did not lose their lives in the location their bodies were found?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So if you find a body with several gunshot wounds without any traces of blood, you consider that they could have been killed on that spot, do you?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: That's quite possible, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Where would the blood be, then? Where's the blood?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: I don't understand, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, how is it possible that there are no traces of blood if there are so many wounds to the body caused by firearms, by gunshot wounds? So those wounds don't bleed, that would mean that.

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: Your Honour, when a person is injured, the wound does bleed, but it doesn't mean that blood will be liberally spread around the scene.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you didn't find blood anywhere. Not liberally spread; you didn't find it anywhere.

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: Sir, I did not observe any blood. It doesn't mean that there wasn't any there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We're going to adjourn now. We're going to adjourn now. Mr. Hendrie, just before we do, help us with this in case some point is going to be made about it hereafter. To what extent did you move any of these bodies when you were examining them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I just overturned -- turned the bodies over, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In your estimation, how soon were you on the scene after death?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't say, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Hendrie, we're going to adjourn for 20 minutes. During the adjournment, please remember not to speak to anybody about your evidence until it's over, and that does include members of the Prosecution team.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will adjourn now for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, based on the information here, I take it that you're a graduate of -- you have a degree in chemistry; right?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me, please, how long does it take, how many hours, for the blood to dry up?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can't answer that question. It depends on a lot of circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Approximately.

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: I can't answer that question, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you know what the circumstances were. So how long? Two hours, three, five, ten hours, more than ten hours?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: Sir, I can't answer that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Suppose the victims were killed on the 15th of January and they stayed there. Can you answer then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would have expected most of the blood to have dried, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: At any rate, the blood should have dried up in the more than 20 hours that lapsed; right?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: I can't answer that, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. When you speak of the crime scene number 3, you describe the body of Ahmet Mustafa, and also you describe in great detail the wounds that he had. This is page 4, paragraph 5. You claim that his body was moved or, rather, turned over and moved from the spot in which it was hit. Can you determine in which spot he was shot?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: I believe that he would -- he'd been killed at that location but had been moved.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you move his body as well?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: I turned his body over, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You claim that this body had no shoes on; right?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But there was a full amount of clothing appropriate to the weather conditions; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: He was fully clothed, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Could one conclude that the footwear was removed from this body before you saw this body?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, do you believe that when somebody leaves the house, that person would put on a jacket, a hat, and so on and then leave the house barefoot? Is that what you normally suppose if you think that the footwear had not been removed from this body?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: Your Honour, people do all sorts of things depending on the circumstances. I cannot tell what was going through this man's mind in the moments before he died.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. As you describe crime scene number 4 and a body identified as Skender, on page 5, paragraph 1, you say that the body was found outdoors and then taken into the house. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: That's what I was told, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who brought the body into the house?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: I wasn't told, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were you able to determine the location in which this person was killed?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: There was a pool of blood and a piece of skull nearby, and that would appear to be the most likely place for the death.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So somebody brought him into the house because, with lacking a fragment of skull, that person could not have entered the house on his own; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: I was told that he had been moved into the house, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you, and when I say "you" I don't mean you personally, I just mean the verifiers, did you keep the axe that was supposedly found and shown to you, the one that you describe on page 4, paragraph 5?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And who showed it to you, this axe?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: There was a gentleman at the scene. I can't recall his name, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: At that time, did you also have some KLA people in -- near you or escorting you?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: There was a KLA soldier, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did somebody take or isolate blood samples from the axe that had been shown to you?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were there any traces of hair on the axe?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: Not that I was able to observe, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So is it your claim that this person was killed with an axe?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In your statement, you claim that you saw a trench which was about 120 centimetres deep and 60 centimetres wide, and about -- over 70 metres long; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: Sir, I'm not very familiar with the metric system. I was using feet. The trench I believe you're referring to was four feet deep and about two feet wide. To answer your question, I did see a trench that would appear to match your description.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So this can be found on page 5, paragraph 3. It was about 120 centimetres deep, 60 centimetres wide, and over 70 metres long; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness has answered that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What could have been the purpose of that trench?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's not for the witness to say. Do you have any idea, Mr. Hendrie?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you also claim that there were no signs that the trench had been recently used; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you examine the entire length of this trench, the entire 70 metres? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, how do you know, then, that there were no traces of recent use?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I saw no traces of recent use.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On page 4, paragraph -- page 5, paragraph 4 in your statement, you describe the crime scene number 5. There was a group of 15 bodies and seven scattered, and you say that this location was taped on a videotape on the 23rd of January between 1329 hours and 1400 hours. Does this mean that this videotape that you mention shows only the location or the bodies as well?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: Just the location, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what is the significance of this footage that was made eight days after the event?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: I wanted to go back to the location to see the actual different positions with more time. On the day in question, I had very limited time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But my question was: What is the significance of this footage of the location which was made eight days after the event?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: On the 23rd, when I returned, I made a record, a fuller record, of the locations where I had not an opportunity previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You say that on the north part of the gully you found casings. How many -- shell casings. How many did you find?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: I didn't count them, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, approximately. Two, four, five, ten, 50?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: There were dozens, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So dozens. So about 50, would you say? And how far from the body were these casings?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: They were a few metres away, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what shells were they? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: I believe they were 7.62 millimetre calibre.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And were the wounds on the bodies caused or inflicted by the shells?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: The majority of the injuries on the bodies that I saw were inflicted by gunshots. I could not say at that time whether the gunshot injuries were caused by weapons fired and then discarding the empty cases I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you find rifle or pistol casings as well?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: The empty cases are typical ammunition from automatic or semi-automatic weapons, not pistols.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Could you be more precise as to the time when you saw these bodies for the first time?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: I didn't make a record of the time. It was shortly before Ambassador Walker arrived on the scene. So if you're aware of that time, then it's possible to get the approximate time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So did he arrive after you?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you said that you arrived at 12.00.

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: About midday, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So that means that he came in the afternoon. You claim that all of the bodies were turned over. Is that true? One can find this on page 5, paragraph 6.

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: I believe I said that the majority of the bodies appeared to be turned over.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Could you describe more specifically what indicated that all of these bodies had been turned over and moved?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: Sir, I said turned over. On the ground next to some of the bodies, there were corresponding patches of blood to the injuries. Some of the bodies had debris, that is dirt and grasses, on their faces which would appear to correspond to the area immediately adjacent to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were you able to determine who had turned over these bodies?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: Categorically, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that all of these bodies had several gunshot wounds, through-and-through gunshot wounds?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: I can't say that all of the bodies had several gunshot wounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On what kind of soil or layer were these bodies lying?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On what kind of surface were these bodies lying? What kind of soil are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: I would merely describe it as dirt, sir. I'm not an expert on soil types, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But when you describe the blood traces, you describe them as pots, not as pools of blood; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: I don't believe I've described pools of blood.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's what I'm saying. You mention patches of blood, not pools of blood.

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: Sir, I believe this is just a matter of semantics. What would be a pool to one person may be a patch to another.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, a patch or a spot indicates just a trace, whereas a pool indicates a larger amount. So I believe that this is not a semantic issue, it's a factual one; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness has made his comment. Let's go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Wasn't it strange to you that despite all these wounds on these bodies that were grouped together there were only patches of blood and not larger amounts of blood that you could call pools of blood? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 6509 to 6513.

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you able to indicate on your photographs and videotapes the traces of blood that you describe? I'm just asking whether you're able to do so, I'm not requiring you to do so right now.

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: I would have to look at the photographs, sir, again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, do you think that you would be able to do that or not, to indicate these traces of blood in the photographs that you made?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: Possibly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Have we got the photographs?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but in that case, I would ask that this time not be counted in the time allotted to me for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll get the photographs out.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether the accused is referring to the photographs shown to this witness during that portion in chief or whether he's referring to all of the photographs in the Racak binder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Any photographs will do. Just produce the photographs taken of the bodies.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The photographs from the crime scenes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes. That would be in Racak binder 1 of 5, and they're here. They're behind tab 5. Could we perhaps have the binder, Racak binder 1, shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So these are the photographs of the ravine in which there were these 15 bodies that you described.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Your Honour, it starts behind tab 5 at number 00732312, and the photographs go through -- well, for some considerable -- two --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Hendrie, can you find the photographs counsel is talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You have.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Does Your Honour want a copy too?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, you're being asked about indications of blood. Perhaps you'd like to look at the photographs. And if you can find one that illustrates what it is you saw, put it on the overhead projector, if you would.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So we are talking about the group that the witness described.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: If I may be of assistance. It's up to the witness, but I do notice that number 54 and 78 seem to describe ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I am referring to the bloodstains on the soil in the location where you found those 15 bodies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness find his way through that bundle and he can produce these photographs to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I wish to remind the witness my question was as follows: Are you able --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Wait a moment. Wait a moment. Let the witness go through the bundle and select the photographs. You can then ask him questions about it later.
