Now, Mr. Hendrie, if you would show us, one by one on the overhead projector, the various photographs which you refer to, and if you want to make any comment about them, do.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, this is photograph ending 352. As you can see, the deceased here has blood or what appears blood on his face, and to the right of his head there is debris and what appears to be blood, which would correspond to the head if he had been rolled over from a face-down position onto his back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Another photograph, 732378. The deceased here at the bottom left-hand corner of the picture, there's a pool, if you wish, of blood, and the body appears to have been -- the rigor mortis set in and would correspond to --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Where is the pool? Could you indicate it with the pointer, please, where the pool of blood that you see is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, go on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Ah. Is that a pool of blood then?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness go on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This area of blood would appear to correspond to the head injury if he had been moved from the face-down position to resting on his back as we see him now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, go on to the next.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The next photograph sir, is 732354. And we see the blood there on the right-hand side of the deceased, with what appears an injury to, as we look at it, the left-hand side of the face. The body, if it was in a face-down position and rolled over from right to left, the blood would correspond to the area of the injury.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can show Your Honour a photograph of a body where it would appear the body has not been turned over and the blood underneath the head would appear to correspond to the injury.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's photograph 732324. The deceased was part of the main group of 15 bodies. The blood underneath the head - and I'd indicate - would appear to correspond to an injury on the deceased's head that we actually cannot see here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Are there any other photographs you wish to say anything about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've not been able to find anything in the short time available, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Do you then, therefore - let's just clear this point up - do you therefore claim that these patches of blood, traces of blood, indicate that the lethal injuries were inflicted on the place in which the bodies were found? Can you say that with certainty?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: Your Honour, nobody can be 100 per cent certain. However, all of the indications are that the deceased died where we found them, albeit that some had been turned over and appeared to have been searched. Documents and personal effects were found next to some of the bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So next to the bodies. They lost their lives there, and next to the bodies were their personal -- documents and personal effects. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: Some of the deceased, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did you perhaps establish who had searched them and turned them over or moved them, brought them in or whatever?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: I did not, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How many casings did you find, whether belonging to shells or pistols, next to scene number 5?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: I believe I said earlier that there were several dozen empty cases a few metres away from the deceased.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In analysing your descriptions and the injuries from 01 to 22 - this is on pages 6 to 9 - it would emerge that these people were hit with a total of 43 bullets, and the wounds inflicted were for the most part in the region of the head, the trunk, the neck, et cetera. Now, in view of all this, the quantity of blood on the scene, on the ground that they were lying on, does this correspond to the number of injuries and anatomic distribution of the wounds on these bodies?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've never actually counted the number of injuries. I was only able to describe the injuries that I saw, and I'm not saying that there were not others.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you're saying that the injuries were caused by firearms mostly; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: It would appear so, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you have any photographs or video footage showing a single case from a rifle that you mentioned a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: I don't recall actually photographing any empty cases. As you might appreciate, sir, I had limited film, and in actual fact, I did run out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You're a professional. You've been a professional soldier for 20-odd years. Is it possible that in your statement you make mention of cases and don't consider it significant to photograph the cases in the places you found them? You say you saw them. Is that logical?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He's a professional policeman. It was translated as "soldier." He's given his answer. He's told you why he didn't photograph them. Now, Mr. Milosevic, you have additional time. Is there anything else you want to ask this witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes, I do have several more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Then let's get on with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On page 7, paragraph 6, you speak of body number 13 and the presence of grasses and dirt stuck to his body. Does that correspond to the surface that the body was found on? I'm referring to leaves and grasses. Where do these leaves and grasses come from in view of the ground, the surface on which the body was found? And I'm referring to body number 13.

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: The location was not consisting purely of bare dirt. There were grasses and other vegetable matter, leaves and such like, lying on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But you can't see that on the photograph at all. On that particular example, the one I'm referring to. There are no leaves or grass anywhere there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can you deal with that or not, Mr. Hendrie? If you can't deal with it, just say so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, I recorded what I saw, and I photographed the bodies in situ. The dirt and debris on the bodies did correspond to the material around the bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you about the leaves and grass.

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: I believe I answered that, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, then. Now, you claim that you were informed that an 18-year-old, Hanemshah Mehmeti, was hit from a sniper somewhere in the village as well as another person who was with her; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And who informed you of that?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: I don't recall, sir, and the name of the person was not recorded. As you might appreciate, not every person that we spoke to did actually want to give their personal details, in view of the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did you talk to her friends and family who transferred her to the house?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: I spoke to whoever was there, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you don't know who with?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: As I said, sir, not all of the people that we spoke to actually wanted to give their details to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And the people you did talk to, were they civilians or members of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: They were all civilians, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When did you leave Racak on the 16th of January?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: About teatime, sir. About 4.00 or 5.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You claim that on the 17th, you had intended to return to Racak. Why was that?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: As you can appreciate, sir, an afternoon to look at the events of the 15th is insufficient, and a return to the scene is always beneficial.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On page 10, paragraph 4, you say that negotiations were held with respect to the entry of Danica Marinkovic, the investigating Judge into the village. Now, what negotiations and who were they conducted with?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: A member of the OSCE, a senior member of the OSCE discussed the matter with the Judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What outcome? What was the outcome?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think we've had evidence about this from the witness. I don't think this witness can help us much more. Mr. Milosevic, you've got ten minutes more, which means you will have had practically an hour and a half with this witness, which is more than enough in the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't need ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, who shot at whom in Racak and the surrounding parts on the 17th of January.

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: From what I saw and the radio communication that I listened in to, it would appear that the security forces laid down fire in the direction of the village. Whether there was any return fire, I cannot say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you happen to know what was going on when the bodies were taken from the mosque, taken over from the mosque in order to be transported to the forensic institute in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what fighting was going on when the judicial organs were taking the bodies from the mosque in order to transport them to the forensic institute or institute for forensic medicine in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And who prevented the investigating Judge not conducting her examination in Racak for a full three days?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: I can't answer that question, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Later on, you attended the work of the forensic team, as far as I was able to gather. Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: At whose invitation were you present during this forensic procedure?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: It was at our request, and the director of the institute acceded to that request.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And were you there when the paraffin glove was taken off the bodies in Racak?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: I was present, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you happen to know the results of those tests?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He's already said that. He didn't.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not with respect to his presence when this was taken. I don't see why he shouldn't be allowed to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He's already said he didn't know the results of the paraffin tests. And anyway, they've been discredited.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So you consider that this has already been discredited, do you? Very well. So the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I was repeating the evidence, which Mr. Milosevic, which this witness had given, which was he didn't know the tests, the results of the tests, and anyway, these sort of tests have not been supported but have been discredited.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the United States, but not in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, does the investigating procedure in Yugoslavia carried out to USA rules or the rules and of the Yugoslav investigating --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, have you any more questions, because you've got less than five minutes left.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Hendrie, I'm first of all interested in one point. When you arrived on that particular day in Racak, were you told, when you were taken to the scene where you saw everything that you saw, were you told at all whether there were any casualties among the KLA on that day? Were there any dead, any fatalities on their part? What do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: I wasn't informed of any KLA casualties at that time. However, I was informed subsequently that the KLA suffered nine casualties.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: While you were performing this job which you went on doing until 4.00 or 5.00 in the afternoon, you didn't know that; right?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And did anybody indicate the spot, just like you were taken to all these other locations, did anybody show you the location of the KLA base on that particular day, where that was?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So you weren't able to see whether there were any traces there of fighting, of blood, or anything of that kind. You weren't able to see that, were you?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: At what point during that day when you finished your work at 4.00 or 5.00 in the afternoon, or, rather, did you know and at what point did you know exactly what the number of casualties was on that day?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: I -- at the end of the day, I was able to tot up the number of bodies that I had seen, but I was led to believe that there were additional casualties that I had not seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Walker was just with you up on the hill, but he didn't go on with you at the end of the day when you ascertained the number of casualties. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: I would not describe Mr. Walker as being with me. He did arrive at the scene with a separate party, and I did not take part or join his group.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your statement, the one you gave, you did not -- and this is on page 5 of the Serbian version, the B/C/S version, you make no mention of this, and it is on page 5, paragraph 2 from the top in the English version. In that portion, you just say that where the 15 -- there were 15 bodies grouped together, you found a grenade casing, a shell casing that you mentioned a moment ago, but you didn't say that you found any casings, in fact, there from automatic weapons. In that statement, that is to say on page 5, paragraph 2 of your statement, you make no mention of having found any casings from a firearm at all.

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not sure which part in the English statement that the counsel is referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Page 5, paragraph 2 from the top in the English version. You just refer to a rifle grenade, and you make no mention in the statement of any cases, casings.

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm now interested in the following, that is to say it refers to page 7 of the B/C/S text and page 7, paragraph 4 of the English version, and onwards. Paragraph 4 onwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: On the spot in the gully, you took note of the position of each body, did you not?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: Generally, yes, sir. There was one exception.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You also took note of the fact that each body, whether it was lying alone or in a group of bodies or one over another, for example, body 9, 10, 12 and 13, you even observed that, made note of that; right?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And you took note of the wounds you encountered. That's right; isn't it?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now, I'm interested in bodies 6 and 7, and that is on page 6 of the B/C/S version and it is page 7, paragraph 2. In the seventh body, you say that the right leg of the sixth body, which was lying next to the man, was near the chest and it appeared that there was some blood from the body of the seventh corpse. The right leg of the sixth body lying next to this man was positioned near the man's chest and appeared to have some blood on his leg from the seventh body. That is what you say in the statement.

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: With the other bodies lying around in a group or one over another, you did not note that there were traces on another body from another corpse. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now, tell me, as an experienced detective, is it possible not to find the traces of one body on another if these people were hit from several bullets, especially in the region of the head, and if they were hit in that spot and if death occurred on the spot, that there would be no body from one -- no blood from one body onto another? How can you explain that? How do you explain the fact that in this group of bodies you found no blood after these shots from one body onto another? Because the blood would have had to have been found on other bodies as well, from one body on another. And in one section here, referring to the tenth body, which was a male, positioned directly below the ninth body, et cetera --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness answer what you've put so far.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would not pretend that my notes and observations were complete and full observation of the scene. It was not practical or possible at that time in those circumstances to treat the examination of the scene as we would like to see at home. The examination was, I admit, hurried, and I recorded as much as I could in the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, there are photographs of all these bodies together. I'm asking you, as an experienced detective working with crimes of this nature, homicide, that's how I'm asking you. What happens to the blood when somebody's shot in the head? Does the blood spurt and splash in different directions? And if so, how is it possible that traces of that blood was not found dispersed on all the bodies? You just found the blood on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We have the point. Now, can you deal with that, Mr. Hendrie, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Each injury or cause of injury is different, depending on the circumstances. Yes, I would have expected to see traces of blood on the other deceased. However, I did not record that. That does not mean it was not there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: We can take a look at the photographs. I've examined them on many occasions and I wasn't able to find what we're talking about. But we have your answer and I don't wish to comment. But I should like to show you, nonetheless, three photographs in the time that I have at my disposal. I'll be able to get through three. Did you see the body of this particular man? It is Racak 2, tab 5.

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm interested in knowing whether he saw him on this photograph where the bodies are separate or on this other photograph where the bodies are grouped together? In the first photograph, they are a good seven or eight metres apart. May we see that photograph, please. Is that the photograph you looked at, this particular scene, rather?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's difficult to see the photograph on the screen. May I have a look at the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, look at it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The photograph shows the position of the bodies when I first saw them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: This next photograph, may we see that one too? And they're all together on that one. Now, which photograph corresponds to the actual state of affairs as it was?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can you help, Mr. Hendrie, or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm trying to recall the actual photograph that I took, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you can't, say so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I -- I believe that the photograph that I took is marked 7614, but I'd have to check my records, sir. Sir, if I may refer you to photograph 732399.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If somebody could find that. Mr. Ryneveld, do you think you can help us with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. 399?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes. Right here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, this photograph shows the scene from a different angle, and I can confirm that I did take this photograph, and it shows the bodies as I did see them. It shows the KLA soldier who was escorting us and two of my colleagues and several of the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So that is separate from the other bodies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic, that seems to have the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hendrie, I have just one more question pertaining to your first statement. You said that the 13th body was below the 11th body. It was on the -- lying on the back with both arms partially stretched out. Can you explain this a bit further? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe the photograph would probably assist more than my recollection of what I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't have the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And, Your Honours, on this witness's second statement, on page 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hendrie, you said the following: I was told that the KLA had removed the bodies of the soldiers before the forces of VJ and MUP had arrived." And then you added the following: "They did so in order to prevent the dead bodies from being publicly shown and used for propaganda purposes." This is what you were told; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And you remember that the person who told you this was a member of the KLA; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: My recollection, sir, is that it was reported to me by one of my team who had been informed by a member of the KLA that that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But you say here that this information was given directly to you by somebody who was a member of the KLA. This is what your statement reflects.

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: Sir, I don't believe that my statement actually reflects that statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, let us move on. We can in fact read what the statement says.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not insisting, Your Honour. Thank you. I'm just interested in the following:

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Your second statement pertaining to Orahovac, page 5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Do you want these photographs any more? Do you want the photographs?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: All right. They can be taken away. We must try and finish this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hendrie, here you speak of some of the information you had regarding Orahovac, and as you say here, you heard that Serb residents of the town were systematically arrested and that the detained include men, women and children. And then you allegedly learned that these missing persons had been killed by the KLA and that there were about 40 of them. Who gave you this information?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: I interviewed a number of the civilian members of the population of Orahovac reporting missing relatives and friends.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: My last question: You say here that: "I was also informed that many of the KLA members involved in the initial detention of the civilian population were members of the local KLA village or town defence unit." So that means that those were civilians. They were what is known as village guards or watches.

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: I can't say whether the members of the KLA involved were actually civilians or true soldiers. I just described it as was described to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Hendrie.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now what is it?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Milosevic, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the English version is here, and what amicus just claimed can be found here. It says here: [Previous translation continues]... "[In English] before the arrival of VJ MUP forces. This was done in order to prevent the case from being displayed and being used --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, we can read.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: And then: "[In English] I am unable to recall how I came to be told this information or the identity of the person who supplied the information. However, I do remember that the source of the information was supposed to have been an UCK member."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We can read that. Yes, Mr. Ryneveld.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Very briefly. I am conscious of the time. Three very quick areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Sir, much has been made during cross-examination about whether or not the bodies in the gully were brought to that location, and you've given your -- your answer and told the Court some of the reasons that -- from which you derived that impression. Did you, in the course of your examination, also make any observations about the clothing and any bullet holes in clothing in relation to wounds?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And how, if at all, did that compare and how, if at all, did that assist you in your conclusion?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: Where the injuries were actually on the torso or arms or legs, the damage to the body corresponded to the damage in the clothing and the corresponding blood.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. Second point: In your experience, sir, if a person is killed outright and the heart stops pumping, do you expect to see more bleeding or less bleeding?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: There would be less, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. About the issue of the drying of blood, you've said it depends on circumstances. Would the depth of the pool of blood be one of those circumstances?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: It could be, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Would the temperature - this is 15th or 16th January - be a factor?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: It would be, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: In your statement, did you notice frost or snow on any of the bodies?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And in your experience, might that also provide drying or provide reliquidation of the blood?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: It could delay the drying of the blood, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Finally, there was questioning about whether you would expect to find blood on adjacent bodies. Assuming that the bodies are upright when shot, in other words point of impact, that's when the spray or blood would be, while they're upright; correct?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: That's what I would expect, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And subsequently when the bodies fall together, if they were together, would you necessarily expect the blood spray to be on the bodies lying adjacent?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Hendrie, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give it. You are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next witness is Mr. Jemini, please. Your Honour, we're back -- there is going to be further Racak evidence but, logistically, it hasn't been possible to have it all together at the same time. Although there's a slightly better scale map in the relevant binder, it may be that the Chamber would be happier continuing to use the atlas for basic geography because the Chamber has become familiar with it. I'll lay this atlas at page 10 on the overhead projector, or have that done. The Chamber will see that Celine, which features in the indictment in respect of deportation rather than specifically in respect of killings, I think paragraph 63 or thereabouts but I'll come to that if necessary in due course, that Celine lies south-east of Bela Crkva and is to be found on page 10 at box K22. Again, waiting for the witness to come in and using the time, unfortunately we don't have an usher to deal with it. Your Honour will probably recall that there are several overhead photographs of Bela Crkva. Perhaps inevitably none of them actually is taken in the direction of Celine, but I can explain by reference to Exhibit 157 where Celine may be found and that will help the process of orientation. First of all, on the map, it's page 10, box K22, Celine south-east of Bela Crkva. And worth noting, there are roads, the red roads, coming from the north, the west, the south; several roads into the village. They feature --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Let the witness come in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your full name, please, sir.

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: Agim Jemini.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Jemini, did you make a statement to investigators of the Office of the Prosecutor in Tirana on the 17th of July of 1999? Did you come to this Tribunal some days ago, and did you, before a presiding officer of the -- appointed by the Registrar, testify -- attest to the accuracy of that statement on the 3rd of June on which day you also provided a short addendum making corrections and amplifications to your statement?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Jemini, before you came in, I'd started the process of assisting the Judges with matters of geography, so I'm picking up a story part way through and there's no need for you to say anything except if I get things wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May I lay on the overhead projector what is Exhibit 157 from the Bela Crkva binder, first of all. I think there are a couple matters of geography that I'll draw to the Chamber's attention on this to save time. The village of Celine is off to the left on this photograph. If we can now focus on -- that's probably all I need ask at this stage. There are other questions I'm going to ask in relation to this photograph for the next witness. The witness, Your Honour, produces two exhibits. Can we distribute them, please. Photographs. I produce them now. It will make more sense of the summary once I read it; that is, the summary of his witness statement. Your Honours, some understanding of the immediate geography of the house in which the witness hid is necessary. I suspect that, although he may be inclined to help us with more detail, survive without knowing the full complexity, but if we do need more detail, there are more photographs available. If we can look at the photographs in order, laying them on the overhead projector, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: They should have exhibit numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 260.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: For both photographs? Thank you. Can we can lay one of the first -- can we lay a colour one, please, on the overhead projector. Take them both.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The first one -- put it on the overhead projector, please. Yes. This shows the view from the window of a partially-completed building, one of, I think, five in the family compound occupied by this witness. The white building ahead is, I think, another building in the compound. But of more significance is the brick -- they're all brick, but the exposed brick building in the foreground which has balconies to it and in which soldiers were stationed during the attack on this village. The witness, from his vantage point, roughly where the cameraman is, being able to overhear what was said by soldiers in the building next door. The next photograph, please. We're now looking back from the opposite side of that compound, towards the house from which the witness was viewing things and in which he was hiding. It is the top exposed square window opening immediately under the roof of that building in which he was positioned and from which he was, in due course, to see the death -- deaths of members of his family. The building to the left of this photograph, the white building, is another building within the compound. But as I say, it may be that detailed local geography is not required because matters are adequately explained in the witness statement and summary. But, Your Honour, I'll ask the witness if I've adequately dealt with those photographs and, if so, may they then become an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Jemini, have I adequately summarised - and it is a summary - the effect of those photographs?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The Chamber will probably have noted, and if not, may I remind it, that there is in this witness's statement a paragraph at page 3 of the statement where the witness gives an account of what he overheard from the adjoining house. The statement is, of course, inevitably to some degree a summary of what he overheard, and having checked this morning, the essence of it is accurate. But it is to some degree the essence, and it may be that the Chamber would prefer the passage that starts: "About 5.00 p.m. that afternoon..." and ending at the following paragraph - a short passage - to be given live by the witness rather than simply read from the statement. I would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In which case, with the Chamber's leave, I will now turn to the summary of the statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We ought to get the statement exhibited.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May we have an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 217 and 217A for the redacted version.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That, of course, incorporates the addendum, I trust. And if the usher would be good enough to put the atlas back onto the overhead projector so that the area can be viewed by those watching. With the -- no, not the overhead photograph, the atlas. I'll hand it in. Here it comes. If the usher would be good enough to put the atlas on the overhead projector, please, where my thumb -- and if the audio-visual unit would focus on the immediate area of Celine and Bela Crkva. The statement of this witness records that, now 40, having lived in the village of Celine all his life with his family, his house was located in a compound of a total of five houses, three of which, including his, were only partly built at the time. The Serb offensive, in his description, was in three phases, of which the first phase occurred at 5.00 on the morning of 25th of March when the village was surrounded with tanks, armoured vehicles, and Pragas. There was, at the time, no KLA presence in the village and none of the villagers had any obvious reason to leave. At about half past five, the Serb forces started to shell and shoot at the village without warning. It appeared at that time they were trying to scare villagers rather than to aim at them. Elderly, women, children, and some men left their homes and collected in open areas within the village which they were unable to leave at the time because it was surrounded. Younger men, fearing they might be targets, decided to hide rather than to gather together with the larger groups. And the witness, with his cousin Isuf, hid in the roof cavity of the incomplete house that I've already shown to you in the photographs. That top level was a level generally unused and he was able to conceal himself within it, being afforded a view from that window space of a large part of the village. Later that morning, a large number of foot soldiers entered the village. The uniforms he's able to describe on page 2 of his statement were of green/brown camouflage uniforms bearing the white double-headed eagle insignia, those in command wearing dark green beret-style hats, the soldiers wearing pointed Partizan-style hats. At about 9.30, a number of soldiers entered the yard of his compound, shot his dog, and started looting the houses, removing valuables. They also removed satellite dishes. Two soldiers who, from what he could overhear, may have been the commanders of the offensive took up positions on the second floor of that adjoining exposed-brick built house that I drew to your attention in the photographs. Additionally, a number of soldiers took up positions in the house in which he was hiding but underneath him and from which they would have had a good view of the village. At about 10.00, the village school was set on fire, and I think burnt down, and throughout the day, he was able to see soldiers looting and setting fire to the houses of the village. Again, they took satellite dishes. Can we now turn in the evidence of the witness himself, and at page 3 of the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Jemini, were you, from your position in the house, able to hear in general conversation between the people in the next-door house? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I should have said that the statement deals with some of the call-signs, Commander 444, and the use of special codes, but the Chamber can read that in detail if it needs to.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Jemini, did you, at about 5.00 in that afternoon, hear something in particular? And if so and in your own time, would you tell us what you heard, please.

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: Yes. We heard a radio conversation where the question was what the situation is like in Celine and the reply was the situation is good. How is it? Is it as well as in Racak? No, it's twice as much as in Racak. At that moment, scared as we were having heard this conversation, we gathered that the number of dead was twice as much as in Racak, approximately about a hundred dead. That was the conversation which we overheard coming via radio communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Later on, at about 7.00, did you hear something else?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: We heard that the offensive at Celine ought to stop, and their commanders agreed that the offensive should stop. And they stopped the offensive at 7.00 in the afternoon -- or in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When you say it was to stop, who said it should stop? Was it somebody in the house or was it somebody over a radio?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: No, it was a command that came from a distance, from remotely, from Prizren where the main command was located and which was in charge of the offensive at Celine, whilst the local commanders in the village agreed to the order that the offensive be stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I return to the summary from which I am reading, with some amplification. Soldiers stayed at points throughout the village that day, although most of them left that night. And at about 8.00 on the morning of the following day, his parents and three other family members returned to the village from where they had been in hiding. He spoke to them. And since people thought that this, the end of what the witness would be describe as phase 1, was the end of the attack generally, they all decided to stay in the village. However, very shortly afterwards, the second phase began with further military units, this time thought by the witness to be special police forces, approached the village from the main road. And as the Chamber will understand, the main road is, of course, the road running north-west/south-east, and to the south of the railway line until just to the east of Celine. So that these soldiers were approaching from that road. There were differences between these and the uniform of the first soldiers. They had coloured ribbons on their sleeves. And as we can see at page 4 of the statement, they had shaved heads, no hats, beards. And the impression obtained by the witness was that they may have been Arkan's men. His mother and father, despite being urged by him to leave the village, remained. His mother, indeed, insisted on baking bread, which in due course was to draw her to the attention of a troop carrier who yelled obscenities at her but on this occasion drove by in the direction of Velika Krusha and Krushe e Madhe, which I think we can see just at the bottom of the screen. His relations went and hid in a basement. He returned, did the witness, to the same roof space, and within half an hour, at about 9.00, there were suddenly 200 to 300 soldiers in the village with coloured ribbons and so on on their sleeves. These soldiers went from house to house, and at about 9.30, they entered his compound and searched every house. When they reached the second floor of the house in which he was hiding, they took up positions, apparently guarding their colleague soldiers who were there. He saw about eight soldiers enter the house in which his parents were hiding in the basement, bring them out and stand them in the yard. He heard the soldiers ask his father and his uncle Shaip if they had money. His father, his cousin Muharrem and his cousin's wife were then taken to the houses in which they had money in order to recover money in a substantial amount, which was then, of course, stolen from them. Those relations were brought back to the witness's mother and uncle. He saw the soldiers lead all five to a gap between the two houses, and he saw them all shot, falling immediately to the ground. A little later, a truck drove into the compound and further looting occurred of property from the houses. And throughout the rest of that day, the witness observed soldiers going around the village, burning houses, using flame-throwers for that purpose and only leaving the newer houses, such as the one in which he was hiding, which were more difficult to burn, intact. Thus it was that his house and the neighbouring house where the commanders were or had been located were not burnt. They also heard, he and his cousin, the sound of automatic gunfire from time to time. The soldiers stayed in the village until about 1.00 the next morning, and as soon as they left, the witness and his cousin left the village, not even feeling that they could check on the bodies of relations whose fate they all-too-perfectly understood. He made his way to Zrze, which the Chamber will remember is to the west of Bela Crkva, the north-west of Celine, and on the way - and one can see the logic of this if the Chamber recalls the site at the junction of the streambed and the railway immediately south of Bela Crkva - on the way, he saw a large number of human corpses there at that junction of the stream and the railway line. That, then, in this witness's account ended the second phase. Having arrived at Zrze at about 5.00 that day, they rested and returned to Celine two nights later - not the four in the statement, that's been corrected in the addendum - and then he with other villagers would spend the days away from the village, returning at night to bury the dead. In the course of this period of time, Serb police together, it would appear, with Gypsies visited the village regularly, looting houses and continuing to burn property. And so it was over the next 30 nights that this witness, as I think I explained, the mayor of his village for many years, or for several years, so it was that he and others returned at night to bury some 78 victims of this attack. Of these 78, some 18 bodies were burnt and carbonised beyond perhaps recognition in many cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Does this appear on the schedule, the victims?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. It's in his statement -- at least I hope it's in his statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, I meant to the indictment. Is this a schedule in the indictment or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Not. For the reasons I've given, that Celine is being dealt with as a deportation site and although, of course, it's all integral to the -- if I'm wrong about that, I'll correct the position. Although it's all integral to really what is a very small area, as we can see from the overhead picture, notwithstanding the awfulness of these events, he might not have been called as a witness but for the very important evidence that he can give about the conversations that were overheard. But I'll just check that he -- that the victims are not in the schedule to the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We will adjourn now. Mr. Jemini, we're going to adjourn for 20 minutes. Would you come back then to conclude your evidence. Remember not to speak to anybody about your evidence until it's over, and that does include the members of the Prosecution team. If the registrar would come up, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to the information you have provided, it says that your previous profession was technical director. Where were you technical director, in fact?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: At the industrial exchange parts in Rahovec.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what is your vocation?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: Mechanical engineering. Mechanical engineering.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And where did you go to school? Where did you graduate and when?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: In Prishtina, in 1985.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that for the last 15 years, you were the head of a village, elected that; is that right? Village leader.

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And who elected you village leader?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: The residents of the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When you were giving your statement to the investigator, you were 38 years old; right?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: Forty years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Forty.

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: Thirty-nine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thirty-nine. Very well. So you were village leader of Celine when you were 24 years old; right?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: From the age of 24.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As this isn't customary in Kosovo, how do you explain the fact that such a young man was elected to be village leader with all the older people around you?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: This can be explained because we were working for the future and the prosperity of the village. And this -- and this was a voluntary position, because every villager tried to contribute something for the future of the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you a member of any political party?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: Now, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Which one?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: The democratic party.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is that the party of Ibrahim Rugova?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who's the president of your party, then?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: Mr. Hashim Thaci.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were you a member of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When did you become member -- a member of the Hashim Thaci party?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: From when the party was founded.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And when was that?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: On the date when it was formed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What was that date?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: On the day when the party was founded, after the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You don't know the exact date?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: No. It's not very important.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'd like you to answer the questions. Now, whether it's important or not is not up to you to decide.

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: Perhaps I can't -- I can't really remember the date but I know that it was founded after the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. On page 2 of your statement, paragraph 2, it says and I quote: "The whole population of the village --"

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I trust the witness has got the statement before him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: "All the inhabitants were still in the village because there were no members of the KLA present, and there was no reason for anyone to leave." End of quotation. Are those your words? "The whole population of the village was still present because we had no KLA presence and there was no reason for anyone to leave." Is that what you say?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, explain this to me: Why do you emphasise the fact that because there were no KLA, that the inhabitants had no reason to leave the village? Why do you say that?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: I say this because everywhere the Serbian army and police entered into areas where there was KLA. So I wanted to say that we were not in any way to blame for this. And that's why we decided to remain in our houses and why nobody left the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But as you say there were no KLA -- we had no KLA presence and there was no reason for anyone to leave the village, when you say that, do you in fact imply that from villages and places in which there were members of the KLA, the population left the villages and those places?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So not even in places where there were KLA members did the inhabitants leave the villages; right?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: Nobody left the villages until Serbian army and police forced them out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I understood your explanation in a different way, that you had no reason because there were no KLA, which means, conversely, that if there were KLA present, the inhabitants had reason to leave the village. Is that logical or not?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: No, because the KLA was in operation for a year. But in no -- nowhere did the population go to Albania in this time. But it was the Serbian army and the police that, according to their strategy, regardless of where the KLA was, it was the Serbian forces that decided to expel the population into neighbouring countries.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. As you say regardless of where the KLA was the Serb forces behaved in the same way, why then did you say that all the inhabitants were still in the village because "we had no KLA presence there"? If this is regardless, as you say, why are you placing it in regard of this, if I can put it that way?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: We emphasised this because, until the NATO intervention, the Serbian army and police had not expelled anybody from the Albanian territories to neighbouring countries. But at the moment of the NATO intervention, they had a strategy ready, prepared, to expel the population regardless of whether the KLA was present in these places or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. That means that before the 24th of March, the beginning of the war, you had no problems. That would follow on from that, would it?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: We didn't have any kind of problem in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then when the war broke out, the refugees started, just like they do in any war; right?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: No. When the Serbian army and police came to the village, whether the KLA was present or not, the intention was to expel the entire population to the territory of neighbouring villages, regardless of who was there. And it involved murders and assaults and arsons and other crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Tell me this: Have you ever heard of a war without refugees?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's not a matter for the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let's first then clear up one other point; what you say in your statement on the first two pages. You explain that the army, at 9.30, arrived. You hid. Various events took place, as you say. They entered houses, took away some property, some belongings. And then on that first day, that is to say, you listened in on a conversation, and then on that first day, they left. Is that right? And you then believed that they had come, gone, and passed through; right?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: Looking at the strategy so far until 25th of March, the army and police throughout Kosova behaved in this kind of way. They would go out and do their duties and then withdraw on single day or half-day offensives. And we, the population, thought it would be an offensive of this kind and we would then be free to return to our homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. As far as I was able to gather, on that first day, the one you're referring to in pages 1 and 2 of your statement, nobody suffered at all; right?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: I think you've misunderstood this. A lot of people suffered on the first day. Fifty-five people were killed on the first day. The entire population was gathered together and robbed at a certain place. Several houses were burned, and there was fire from tanks and armoured vehicles and Pragas throughout the day. From 6.00 in the morning to 8.00 in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You say from 5.30, but that doesn't matter. And where does it say in your statement that people did fall casualty on that first day? You didn't write that anywhere. You didn't say that anybody was a victim on that first day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Let the witness deal with that. Just look at your statement, Mr. Jemini, if you have it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. In my statement, it says like that. But the murders of the 25th happened on that day, when -- and it was on -- at 8.00 in the morning that the news came that so many people had been killed, on the following day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, come on now, please. Show me in your statement, where you begin with the 25th of March at 5.00 and then 5.30, you say: "About 5.30 a.m., the military forces..." That is in paragraph 3 on the first page. "It did not appear that they were aiming at the people but it seemed that they were trying to scare everyone in the village." That is how your sentence reads. And then you go on to say that people left and so on. But nowhere on the first day do you speak -- there is absolutely no statement of yours referring to any people getting hurt or any casualties or any individuals getting hurt. Isn't that right? And then they left, you say, and returned afterwards. That's another matter. But as to that first day, tell me, please, where in your statement does it say that people were hurt, that there were casualties?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: In my statement, it states what happened on the 25th and the 26th and the 27th and thereafter. It says very clearly what happened on the 25th. The 26th -- and please read my statement carefully.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, precisely because you say specifically what happened, I claim that your statement makes no mention of anybody getting hurt on the 25th. Is that right or is it not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The accused is simply not turning to his mind to what the evidence has been. 5.00 p.m. the same day, the witness has already given an account of what he overheard, the inference he drew from that, and if he didn't happen to see any particular killings because of his vantage point, that's one thing, but it's clear as can be that he assumed right from the beginning that there were killings going on and he gave a calculation of how many he thought there were from what he overheard on the radio.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That is right. Nowhere it refers to 55 people. If it does, perhaps you could refer me to it. Now, Mr. Milosevic, you've made the point. Let's move on to something else.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, this fact that nothing happened on that first day logically refutes what you're talking about when you say that you listened in, that you heard this; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. That's not a point. The witness has described what he heard, and you can ask him about it, but asking him hypothetical questions like that is not going to help anybody.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll ask him now. I'll ask him about that right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How far is this house away, the one you indicated from which you allegedly listened in to the conversation which the commander had via radio with the person he was communicating with? How far is this house?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: Fifteen metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, can't you see on this photograph, as you can see your own window from which this was taken, that it's at least 50 metres to that house?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We have --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. That's what you may think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We have the photograph in front of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And on the photograph, can you see that there's no window facing you, towards you?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: No. It seems you don't understand the photograph, because 0226138, you can see the window clearly with two balconies in front. So you can see that it's only 15 metres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The balconies are not facing you, are not turned towards you, neither are the windows. They don't face you, they are at an angle of 90 degrees and are facing the direction from which your window was looking out onto, but there's no window facing you. So you claim that you were listening to a conversation taking place in the neighbouring house which has no windows turned towards you and that you were doing this, to boot, from the loft, the attic of a neighbouring house, which is the distance you can see, and we can establish that distance. We're not going to go into that now. But you claim that you were listening in to this conversation via radio.

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: Excuse me. We know that you don't accept the truth, but the truth is that the window is in the position to see the two balconies, a distance of 15 metres. It's not -- it's not a photograph of the kind that you suggest at all. So you can indeed see this site from 15 metres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But these are balconies that have not been finished yet. Construction not completed. People couldn't sit out on them. And the people were inside and you say that you heard their conversation from your window where you were hiding so that nobody could see you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That is his evidence, yes, that he could hear the conversation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But according to the statement from the alleged crimes that he refers to, part of the satellite dish was removed from the building. And he says that he heard how there would -- it would be worse in Racak. And then he heard them say, "Stop the attack on Celine," and the other man said, "Yes, we will," as if this was a conversation between the command and the officers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is not a question. Either you must ask a question or we'll close the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. I'll move on. I'll move on in my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On page 2, paragraph 2, you say that most of the inhabitants left their homes and collected at two or three main areas in the village. Which areas were these?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: These are on the outskirts on the village where they felt they were safer. Places of hiding, in the shade of -- at the foot of a mountain or hiding in some kind of hole where bullets wouldn't be able to catch them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And why didn't you go with them there? Why didn't you collect there but you hid in the attic with a relative of yours? Why were you hiding in the attic?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: We didn't leave because we knew what the Serbian strategy consisted of, and we were quite aware of what they thought of people who were involved in contributing to the prosperity of their country, especially belonging to the ages of between 30 and 40 years of age. And we were interested not to be amongst women and children and the elderly, our mothers and fathers, so that they wouldn't become subject of mistreatment. That is why we preferred to remain at a distance so that we wouldn't testify to the worst. I can say that at the moment when everybody left the village of Celine, I personally, as village chief, I personally -- there was people, two people came and were beaten up because they couldn't tell the police and the army where I was. They inquired about my whereabouts, and they were unable to tell them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And why were they looking for you, especially when you weren't a KLA member?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: It's not true that the Serb -- that the strategy of Serbian police and the army was to inquire after KLA members. Part of their brief for years on end was to eradicate everything that is intellectual and contributes to the prosperity of the Albanians. That's what Serbian criminals attempted to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Will you please just answer my questions. We don't need to go into this business with intellectuals. Why did you hide in the attic with your relative --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: -- and you didn't know where your children were?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If the accused asks questions of the kind he asks of a person who may rank as an intellectual and the person's understanding is that he may have been targeted on that basis, then the answer is proper. And the accused regularly trying to shut out questions by making comments is really unacceptable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Next question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I didn't understand this witness to be an intellectual, and if it is true --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're not going to go into this now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've dealt with it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So now, as you just described to us, everybody had left except for you and your relative who were in the attic. And where were your children at that moment?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: At that moment, my children, my father, my mother, and my wife, they -- alongside the rest of the extended family and the overall inhabitants of Celine, went away together. As I said earlier, we did not want to be in their midst, being aware that your police, based on the strategy that we were fully aware of what it was, wouldn't want to be a part of that, because it wasn't only me and my cousin; there were other people who were left behind and helped bury the people and the victims of the massacre that occurred at Celine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain to me, please, where did the army shoot at the village from?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: It's not a big deal. It wasn't choosing its positions. The whole village was encircled from all sides. From the main road, Prizren, Gjakove, from Bellacerkva, from Rahovec, from Lignaci, from Krushe e Madhe.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And if they were not targeting people in the village, then what did they target?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: No. They appeared keener to secure their entry on foot into the village so that everybody would be massacred and there'd be burning down. So their duty on the first day, using heavy artillery, was to pave the way for the entry the very next day of the infantry and of the soldiers on foot to do everything that does not belong to modern civilisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what did they destroy with their artillery in order to clear the way?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: Nothing else but to scare the population away so that it would be easier for them to carry out what they'd set out to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You say that you were hiding for 48 hours in the attic with your cousin Isuf Jemini. Did Isuf give a statement to the investigators of the Tribunal as well?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: Yes. But given that the statement was fairly similar, given we were together all the time, it appeared sufficient to have only one statement of that kind submitted before this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In your statement, you say: "In the house adjacent to us, commanders used second floor and balcony on the second floor, the balcony which faced the house in which I was hiding." So as we can see from this photograph, this balcony is not facing the house, it's facing the opposite side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we've been over this point. We're not going to go over it again. Find another point.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You claim that the soldiers shot indiscriminately throughout the village, broke into houses, looted, yelled, and so on; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So that means that they were shooting indiscriminately and yelling and so on. So all of that must have produced a lot of noise. Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: Not necessarily a lot of noise. It -- it was quiet because the population was not there and it was only the Serbian military and the police that operated in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, everything that you listed so far, didn't that create a lot of noise? Now you're telling us that it was quiet in the village. So what was it? Was there noise, yelling, shooting, and everything that I've numbered so far, or was it quiet? Choose one or the other.

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: No. The noise and the shouting came from the side of the police and the army. There was no noise made by the population of that village because they were waiting death to come.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about the origin of the noise. I'm just asking you whether all of that shooting, yelling, and so on, did that produce a lot of noise? You are telling us that the army did all this. So was there a lot of noise?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: Yes, certainly there was some noise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Could you now explain to me, please, how was it possible that you were in the attic, hiding, and all of this noise created by the army and firing was going on by the army and all the while you were able to hear the conversation in the adjacent house.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, the question, to be fair, should be this: Was there -- was there a noise at the time of the conversation?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: The noise was coming from the village. It wasn't concentrated where we and the Serbian police, 15 minutes away from us, was situated. So the noise came remotely from the village. And that did not hamper us overhearing the conversation that the police carried out during those moments.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And in your statement, on page 3 you say as follows: "I watched the whole day the soldiers go into the houses throughout the village." So were you able to see that through that same window?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: Excuse me. Maybe you're misreading the third part of this declaration. That came after we'd been to Xerxe and returned two days later. And then we stayed in the village for about 30 days, on the outskirts of the village, that is, where we buried all the people that had been killed and massacred. All in all, 82 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to read to you paragraph 2 on page 3. It says as follows: "Throughout the day ..." so now you describe how you were hidden up there for 48 hours. This is on page 3, paragraph 2. And you say: "Throughout the day, I saw soldiers entering and looting all the houses of valuables throughout the village. They removed satellite dishes from all of the houses. During the day, 12 houses were set on fire," and so on. So this means that you watched the entire day how the soldiers entered the houses in the whole village.

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: Yes. This happened on the 26th. Throughout the day on that day, they entered the houses and looted, took away all valuables and demolished everything that was deemed to be demolishable.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please. You are now referring to the 25th. The 26th will not begin until the end of that page when you say: "About 8.00 a.m. the next day, my parents," and so on and so on.
