So what you spoke of before was the 25th. So how was it possible for you to see from this window during the course of the entire day the soldiers entering the houses and so on? What were you able to see from that window?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: As I've mentioned in the statement -- or I mentioned in the statement everything I was able to observe throughout the day from 8.00 in the morning until the evening, beginning from the first meeting with the parents, then the Serbian police killing my parents, and proceeding likewise until evening when I observed police and the army entering every single house and burning it down. Until the hours of the evening, that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Jemini. Mr. Jemini, please take a look at your statement. While you are describing what happened during the day of 25th, you said: "Throughout the day, I saw soldiers entering and looting all the houses." So you are being asked about that sentence, about that paragraph. Is it that you watched all of that, all of what happened during the day, or is it the kind of thing you've heard of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I saw everything throughout the day on the 25th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So the question is that -- whether you are able to see all the village from the window of the room you were hiding in.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We had that vantage point which enabled us to see not only from that window but also from other parts of the roof. We could take away the tiles and be able to see what was happening around the village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please go on, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. So that means that there was a military command 15 metres from you, a full yard of people, of soldiers, as well as the second storey of the house, and yet you still take the roof tiles off the roof in order to look. So weren't you afraid that you would be noticed?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: Yes. However, we thought we were capable of that, and we felt ourselves superior to the Serbian army which had broken up all rules and sent soldiers to occupy the second floor of my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. I'm talking about your fear now. You hid out of fear, not because you wanted to be above, on a storey above. Weren't you afraid to remove the roof tiles of a house in which there were a lot of troops as well as a yard full of troops? Weren't you afraid of being noticed?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: Yes. At that moment, fear appeared to be going away, because we were expecting to be killed from moment to moment, having seen what was happening around the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. That is quite enough. Now, tell me, please, paragraph 1, page 3, you state there that the soldiers who were on the second floor of the house in which you were hiding just a few metres above, in the attic, stood guard for the rest; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How did you conclude that? Why would they stand guard if there was nobody else in the village except for armed residents and especially in view of the fact that there were no armed KLA members, as you claim it? So why did they have to stand guard?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: This is a fact. In fact, they thought that there was nobody. In fact, there were two of them were only a few metres away. We were on top of that. We could have done everything; we could have killed them. We could have killed the command and everybody else. We didn't do that because we did not believe in that kind of method in this kind of civilisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were you armed?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So how could you have killed them if you were not armed, killed the commander and the soldiers and so on?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: There were ample opportunities to kill them. There were other methods. You can't kill people using weapons alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, what other methods were at your disposal? Could you please tell us?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is all hypothetical. Mr. Milosevic, you've got two minutes left. Is there anything else you want to ask this witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have many more questions left. And I can't see why do I have to cross-examine this kind of witness for less than 40 minutes, Mr. May. He is coming out with all kinds of things here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We have judged it -- we judge that 45 minutes is sufficient. Now, if you have anything else to ask him, you should ask it now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have at least 30 more questions. But let me try and complete this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say here that specialist troops came. They had beards and they had red ribbons. They were armed in a similar way. They had long knives that were at least half a metre long. Does that mean they had some kind of sabers?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: You should know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But this is what you're claiming. I don't know of these knives that are more than half a metre long. That's what I'm asking you, were they in fact sabers? And then you say that they saw your mother in the yard and said, "Well, what are you doing there, old woman?" And at that time you were hiding with your cousin in the attic. So my question is: Why were you hiding under the roof when even your mother, a female therefore, stood in the yard, baked the bread, and went on her normal business?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: It is not true that life was carrying on as normal. She had come over to bring us some food. However, being aware of the plans of the Serbian offensive, I told her to return and join the rest of the population, to join everybody else, my wife, the children. So I wanted the same of my parents. I was aware of the impending offensive of the day. And my wife -- my -- excuse me. My -- correction. My mother returned with her bread in her hands, and when she came, there were 12 Serbian police brought a truck which was driving by our yard. They saw my mother, and in barbarian Serbian language, they spoke to her and she was scared away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What -- we're bringing this examination to an end. You're now past your time. But tell us this, Mr. Jemini: What happened to your mother?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My mother and father and the cousins were in the basement. So when my mother went there, she said she'd seen a group of Serbian police. And they decided to stay or to re-enter the basement. But at that very moment or 10 or 15 minutes later, police went in -- Serbian military police went into the yard. They demolished all the doors and decided to go inside the houses. They went into the basement, seven or eight of them, and they took out of the basement seven members of my family; my mother, my father, my uncle, and his son with her [sic] wife. They were ordered to stay in front of the houses but - you see by the photographs that have been submitted as evidence - at that moment, the policeman asked my parents whether they had any money. My father says yes he has got some money. Where are they? In the bedroom. And -- of the building where they were. And my mother says in Albanian, "What do you want of us old people? We've got nothing against you, nothing against you carrying out your duties. We've done nothing wrong. So please go out and carry your duties against those that you think are undermining you or acting against you. So leave us alone." The other policeman intervenes in Serbian and says: "You shut up because nobody is asking you." The first policeman asks Muharrem, my cousin, whether he has any money and he says yes. And he asked where were they, and he said in the house to the rear. And without any hesitation, they say they would return to their houses in order to get the money. Some moments later, however, all of them were put together at the house opposite, about five or six metres away, the one that is five or six metres away, and then they make them face the wall and, from a pistol gun -- a pistol arm was shot in the air first and then with an automatic gun rifle, they were shot at and they fell. That is the moment when calamity fell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please. I would like to remind you of the part of your statement, page 4, paragraph 8 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We have gone past the time which we can sit and I brought your cross-examination to a close. Mr. Milosevic, you must concentrate on asking relevant questions, and you must stop arguing with the witnesses. That way, you'll get through very much more. We're going to adjourn now. I'm afraid there's no time for re-examination or anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was going to make this observation, though, that in his 45 minutes of cross-examination of a man who says he's lost and seen the loss of his parents under gunfire in a very substantial alleged massacre, the accused hasn't actually put a case and the 45 minutes really has taken us nowhere. And I'm going to count it, for the purposes of argument, as evidence that is unchallenged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're dealing with a litigant in person. We're dealing with a litigant in person, Mr. Nice, and therefore, various different considerations apply. Mr. Milosevic, we've -- we are adjourning now. We will deal with matters in the morning on Monday. Mr. Jemini, thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give evidence. It's now concluded. You are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to put in an objection to this cross-examination, especially to what Mr. Nice just said, because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You've heard our response. We have replied to Mr. Nice. We're not going to take the matter any further. We will adjourn now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 10th day of June, 2002, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.45 p.m.,
